did_you_know.text: Did you know? Chapter 3 opens with a personal, first-person description: "I am the man who has seen affliction." The speaker presents his suffering as torment brought upon him under the rod of God's wrath.
Did you know? The description of suffering in this chapter includes not only outward pain, but also a sense of ongoing affliction: "Surely against me he turns his hand again and again, all day long."

Did you know? The speaker compares himself to a target at which arrows are aimed: "He bent his bow and set me as a target for his arrows." This image emphasizes his sense of being wounded and pursued.
Did you know? After describing his suffering, the speaker turns to memory and asks the Lord to remember his affliction and wandering, described through images of wormwood and gall.

Did you know? At the center of the chapter, hope emerges: alongside the memory of his distress, the speaker declares that the Lord's steadfast love has not ended and His mercies have not come to an end.

Did you know? The chapter teaches the goodness of waiting for and seeking the Lord: "The Lord is good to those who wait for Him, to the soul that seeks Him." Hope is presented as a process of waiting and seeking.
Did you know? Bearing the yoke is described as an experience that has its place even in youth: "It is good for a man to bear the yoke in his youth."
Did you know? After describing suffering and hope, the chapter calls for active self-examination: "Let us examine and test our ways, and return to the Lord."
Did you know? Even from "the lowest pit," the speaker continues to call on the Lord. In response to his cry, the Lord is described as one who hears, draws near, and says, "Do not fear."

Did you know? At the end of the chapter, the speaker asks the Lord to repay his enemies according to their deeds. Thus, the chapter ends with a plea for judgment and recompense, following its descriptions of suffering, repentance, and deliverance.
